title: Indian Markets Are Closed Today for Bakrid. When They Reopen, June Will Be a Stock-Picker's Market. Here Is Where the Smart Money Is Moving.
excerpt: Foreign investors have pulled $24.3 billion out of India this year. Domestic funds are absorbing every dollar. The May derivatives series ended flat. June will reward selectivity over momentum.
body:
Indian stock exchanges — the BSE and the NSE — are closed on Wednesday, May 28, for Bakri Id. When trading resumes on Thursday, the market enters a new derivatives series with a fundamentally different character than the one that just ended.

The Nifty 50 closed the May series at 23,913.7 points, essentially flat after months of gut-churning volatility driven by the Iran war and the energy shock that followed. The Sensex sits at 75,867. Both indices have fallen roughly 5 to 7 per cent since the conflict broke out in February, and foreign investors have pulled out $24.3 billion in 2026 alone — surpassing the record annual outflows seen last year.

But here is the number that matters more: domestic institutional investors have bought $25 billion worth of Indian equities this year. For every dollar the foreigners have sold, domestic money has bought more than a dollar back. The Great Decoupling, as market analysts are calling it, is no longer a thesis. It is a fact.

What June Looks Like

Two major brokerages — Systematix and Axis Direct — have published their June outlooks, and both agree on the broad shape. The Nifty is expected to trade in a 23,000 to 25,000 band, with 24,000 as the key pivot point. The market is transitioning from a short-covering-led recovery to fresh positioning at higher levels. In plain language: the panic selling is over, but the broad-based rally is not coming back either.

June will be a stock-picker's market. That means sector rotation, not index momentum, will drive returns. Domestic institutions are moving selectively into metals, infrastructure, and defence, while staying cautious on IT and banking — two sectors that have borne the brunt of the FII exodus.

For NRI investors with PIS accounts and Indian mutual fund holdings, this shift has practical implications. If your portfolio is weighted toward large-cap index funds that track the Nifty, you are essentially flat for the year. If you are in actively managed mid-cap or thematic funds focused on domestic consumption, infrastructure, or energy transition, you may be outperforming the headline indices by a wide margin.

The Oil Premium Is Not Going Away

Brent crude rose more than 3 per cent this week to nearly $100 per barrel after the US-Iran ceasefire began to unravel. Fresh American airstrikes on Iran and retaliatory IRGC attacks have pushed any prospect of reopening the Strait of Hormuz further into the future. Asia bought roughly 80 per cent of the oil that used to flow through the strait, and India — which imports more than 80 per cent of its crude — is one of the most exposed economies on the planet.

Goldman Sachs is now forecasting another 50 basis points of rate hikes by the Reserve Bank of India, driven by imported energy costs, fiscal pressure, and current account deterioration. The rupee, already at record lows, slipped further this week as hopes of an imminent peace deal faded.

For NRIs, this creates a strange duality. Your dollar-denominated income buys more rupees than ever, making remittances, property purchases, and NRE deposits more attractive. But the companies in your Indian portfolio are paying more for energy, facing higher borrowing costs, and watching their margins compress.

SEBI Is Rewriting the Options Playbook

In a move that received less attention than it deserved, the Securities and Exchange Board of India published a proposal this week to overhaul how options strike prices are set during volatile trading sessions. The current system leaves traders without suitable contracts when prices move sharply — exactly the kind of environment that has defined 2026.

Under the new framework, exchanges will be required to introduce new strike prices in real-time during sharp market moves, review strike price availability daily, and remove contracts that are far from current levels. The proposal also aims to standardise rules between the NSE and the BSE, which currently follow different strike price methodologies.

SEBI has invited market feedback by June 15. If implemented, the changes would make Indian derivatives markets more liquid and responsive during periods of war-driven volatility — precisely the kind of environment NRI options traders have been navigating all year.

The Quiet SEBI Power Grab

A separate SEBI panel is proposing tighter oversight of how companies use funds raised through equity offerings. The proposed rules would give credit rating agencies direct reporting lines to stock exchanges, introduce penalties for non-cooperation, and lower the threshold at which mandatory fund-use monitoring kicks in. The framework mirrors the UK's model, where investment banks are required to track IPO proceeds.

For NRI investors who participate in Indian IPOs — and a growing number do, given the recent liberalisation of PIS limits — this is a governance upgrade that reduces the risk of capital misallocation, a chronic concern in Indian primary markets.

What to Watch in June

Oil prices. If Brent holds above $95, expect the RBI to stay hawkish and the rupee to remain under pressure. If a ceasefire reopens Hormuz, Indian markets could rally 5 to 8 per cent in a matter of days.

FII positioning. Foreign investors have now reduced their average India allocation to 9.94 per cent — below 10 per cent for the first time since January 2021, and down from 17.47 per cent in August 2024. The question is whether this is capitulation or the beginning of a longer structural underweight.

Domestic SIP flows. Systematic investment plans have been the backbone of the Great Decoupling. India's mutual fund industry recently crossed ₹82 lakh crore in assets. As long as SIP inflows remain strong — and they show no signs of weakening — the domestic bid will continue to absorb foreign selling.

The Nifty's 50-day moving average. The May series ended with the index stalling near this technical level. A clean break above it in June would confirm the transition from recovery to fresh positioning. A rejection would signal more range-bound trading.

The Bakrid holiday is a pause, not a pivot. But when Indian markets reopen, the game will have changed. The era of riding the index is over. June belongs to those who can pick.
